title: For all
example: If S = {2, 4, 6} and P(x) means “x is even”, this is true.
note: ∀ means every, so one counterexample makes the whole statement false.
wrong: At least one x in S makes P(x) true.
No x in S makes P(x) true.
Exactly one x in S makes P(x) true.

title: There exists
parts: There is at least one x
example: In {1, 2, 3}, there is an even number: 2.
note: The colon means “such that” here, not division.
wrong: Every x in S makes P(x) true.
Exactly one x in S must make P(x) true.
P(x) is false for every x in S.

title: Exactly one exists
example: There is exactly one integer x with x + 2 = 5: x = 3.
wrong: There is at least one x, possibly many, with P(x) true.
Every x makes P(x) true.
There is no x that makes P(x) true.

title: Implication
example: If it is a square, then it has four sides.
note: This does not say q implies p. A false premise does not make the implication false.
wrong: If q is true, then p is true.
p and q are both false.
p is true and q is false.

title: If and only if
example: An integer is even if and only if it is divisible by 2.
note: Both directions must hold: p ⇒ q and q ⇒ p.
wrong: Only p implies q; the reverse need not hold.
Exactly one of p and q is true.
p and q must both be true.

title: Logical AND
note: AND may also appear as && in code, or a dot in Boolean algebra.
wrong: Only the truth of p is required.
Exactly one of p and q must be true.
At least one may be false while the statement still holds.

title: Inclusive OR
parts: q is true (or both are true).
example: x = 2 satisfies “x is even OR x is positive”, since both are true.
note: Mathematical OR is inclusive unless stated otherwise.
wrong: Exactly one of p and q is true.
Both p and q must be true.
Neither p nor q is true.

title: Logical negation
parts: It is not the case that
example: If p is “5 is even”, ¬p is true.
wrong: p is definitely true.
p implies itself.
p and another statement are true.

title: Exclusive OR
parts: q is true: exactly one is true.
example: True ⊕ True = False; True ⊕ False = True.
note: XOR differs from OR when both inputs are true.
wrong: At least one is true, including when both are true.
Both are true.
Neither is true.

title: Set membership
example: 3 ∈ {1, 3, 5} means 3 is one of the members.
note: ∈ compares an element with a set; ⊆ compares sets.
wrong: x is a subset of S.
S is an element of x.
x is not in S.

title: Subset
example: {1, 2} ⊆ {1, 2, 3}. A and B may also be equal.
note: ⊆ allows equality. We use ⊊ for a proper subset.
wrong: A and B have no shared elements.
A must contain B.
A is one individual element of B.

title: Union of sets
note: Union is the set version of inclusive OR.
wrong: Only elements in both A and B.
Elements in A but not in B.
Ordered pairs from A and B.

title: Intersection of sets
note: Intersection is the set version of AND.
wrong: All elements in either A or B.
Elements in A but not B.
The number of elements in B.

title: Set difference
note: Set difference is directional: A ∖ B can differ from B ∖ A.
wrong: Elements shared by A and B.
Elements of B excluding A.
Every element of either set.

title: Cardinality of a set
parts: The number of elements in the set S.
note: Bars mean cardinality for a set, but absolute value for a number.
wrong: The largest number in S.
The sum of all elements in S.
The absolute value of every element in S.

title: Set builder notation
note: ℤ includes negative integers, zero and positive integers. The condition filters them.
wrong: All real numbers greater than zero.
All integers less than zero.
Only the integer zero.

title: Cartesian product
parts: and pair it, in order, with
an element from B, for every possible pairing.
note: This is a Cartesian product, not numerical multiplication of sets.
wrong: Elements that appear in both sets.
The union of the two sets.
Only pairs whose two elements are equal.

title: Power set
parts: The set of all subsets of S.
note: The empty set and S itself are both included.
wrong: The probability that S occurs.
The set of individual members of S only.
The largest subset of S only.
